(g)the third country protects and promotes human and labour rights, including by implementing the United Nations Global Compact and the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights as well as respecting international law;

(h)the inclusion of the third country does not entail a risk of circumvention of the Union origin requirements set out in this Regulation, in particular through the re-export of products or components originating in third countries, or through the establishment on its territory of undertakings owned and controlled by entities established in third countries that are not within the scope of this Article with the purpose to access to the Union market for such products or components.

ev.justification: This amendment makes the recognition of third-country content as being of Union origin subject to clear conditions safeguarding reciprocity, fair competition, the Union’s economic security and climate commitments, while preventing circumvention. It extends this approach to both public procurement under Article 11 and public support schemes under Article 12, requiring national treatment for Union products or entities where comparable measures or schemes exist in the third country. Recognition must be withdrawn where the conditions are no longer met. For third countries meeting the additional criteria set out in points (i) to (iv), the amendment establishes a binding three-month deadline for the adoption of the relevant delegated acts, provided that all substantive conditions are fulfilled. This provides predictability for trading partners and businesses and supports timely implementation without weakening the safeguards governing eligibility.

It is considered appropriate to introduce a mechanism ensuring that the European content requirements laid down in the IAA are aligned with the EU’s industrial capacity, to avoid a mismatch between policy objectives and available manufacturing capacity. Bringing the different requirements into force before a competitive supply base is in place could have the opposite effect. Accordingly, the minimum thresholds should not create bottlenecks or disproportionate cost increases that could undermine project competitiveness. The targets should be phased in progressively in line with European production capacity, which should be monitored in advance and strengthened through policies supporting investment and industrial development. To that end, a mechanism shall be established to assess developments concerning each product, material or component falling within the scope of the IAA and, where necessary, to adjust the applicable Union-content percentages. Such adjustment may also take the form of allocating the required percentages across different geographical tiers, comprising the Union, the European Economic Area and third countries that grant reciprocal market access to Union products and comply with quality, environmental and labour standards equivalent to those applicable in the Union

ev.amended: 2a.The determination of origin shall not be circumvented through minimal processing or assembly operations that do not confer origin under Regulation (EU) No 952/2013. Compliance checks shall, where relevant, cover the origin of components subject to a specific requirement under this Regulation and shall use existing customs and product documentation wherever possible. For steel, available information identifying the country where it was first melted and poured shall be used for verification where relevant and proportionate, without replacing the applicable origin rules or the equivalent treatment provided for in Articles 8 and 9. The same evidence shall not be requested again where it is already lawfully available to the competent authority.
ev.justification: European-origin requirements must reward genuine manufacturing rather than superficial assembly. Melt-and-pour evidence can support proportionate verification without replacing origin rules, disrupting partner equivalence or duplicating documentation.

ev.amended:
2a.Notwithstanding paragraph 2, and solely for the purposes of this Regulation, a product or component shall be considered to be of Union origin only if it meets both of the following conditions:
(a) it underwent its last substantial processing in the EU, within the meaning of Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013;
(b) the value added represents at least 60 % of the ex-works price, calculated in accordance with the definition provided in Article 3 of this Regulation.
Operations involving a minor transformation, and therefore not in accordance with Article 3, shall not be sufficient to confer Union origin under this Regulation, regardless of their contribution to Union added value.

2a.For the purposes of this Chapter, products and components shall be treated as content of Union origin if they are wholly obtained in an overseas country or territory listed in Annex I to Council Decision (EU) 2021/1764, or if they are manufactured there exclusively from materials of local or Union origin, provided that:
(a) the installation is not controlled by an entity established in a third country referred to in Article 11(1);
(b) the applicable social, labour and environmental law, and the fundamental conventions of the International Labour Organisation, are complied with.
This treatment shall be without prejudice to Union customs legislation.
ev.justification: Overseas countries and territories are part of Member States and are not third countries. This treatment is limited to local resources and the processing of those resources locally with a view to supporting local employment and preventing the territories concerned, which are located outside the customs territory, from being used to circumvent the origin requirements.

The present amendment seeks to supplement Article 7(1), as amended, by introducing a specific paragraph on holistic “Made in EU” criteria for certifying European origin in relation to certain technologies used in large-scale infrastructure projects. Responsibility for monitoring compliance with these criteria would lie with the Member States, which are directly involved in their delivery through public procurement, State aid and other instruments. This would allow them to assess the appropriate level of ambition on a project-by-project basis, taking into account the specific characteristics and assets of the local nuclear ecosystem.

ev.amended: 2a.The Commission shall maintain a single, publicly accessible and regularly updated electronic list of third countries, sectors and product categories in respect of which content is treated as equivalent to Union origin under this Regulation. The list shall clearly identify the date from which such treatment applies and any sectoral or product-specific limitation. Economic operators may rely on such treatment by identifying the relevant content and country in the self-declaration or equivalent document used for the purposes of this Regulation. No prior individual authorisation or additional application shall be required where the applicable conditions are met.
ev.justification: Make partner-country treatment genuinely easy to opt into. A company should be able to check one authoritative list, identify the relevant content in its existing declaration and rely on the rule. It should not be necessary to interpret several delegated acts or apply separately for equivalent-origin treatment.

ev.amended: 2a.The Union origin requirements and third-country equivalence rules laid down in this Chapter shall be applied in accordance with the Union's obligations under WTO agreements and international agreements concluded by the Union. The Commission shall regularly assess compliance of the implementation of this Chapter with those obligations. It shall report its findings to the European Parliament and the Council. The Commission shall publish and keep data guidance on the relevant coverage of those obligations.

2a.The Union origin requirements do not apply to projects for which an auction has been announced, a support scheme was established or the application for support was submitted before the date on which the relevant requirement under Annex II came into effect, even if the procurement of the final product or its main specific components takes place after that date. The update of an existing support scheme shall result in the application of the new requirements only if it alters the eligibility conditions for the final products receiving support.

2a.By six months after the entry into force of this Regulation, the Commission shall review the definition of last substantial, economically justified processing or working laid down in Article 169 of Regulation (EU) 2026/2108 for products and components covered by this chapter with the aim of including at least 50% of added value originating in the Union for those products and components and preventing the circumvention of the rules on the acquisition of origin.

2a.The Commission shall review the application, to products and components covered by this Regulation, of the rules determining the last substantial transformation referred to in f Regulation (EU) No 2026/2108, with a view to preventing circumvention of the Union origin requirements laid down in this Regulation and ensuring genuine value creation within the Union, while taking into account the specific characteristics and realities of the relevant supply chains.

2a.By way of derogation for aluminium products, origin shall be determined based on the country where aluminium is first produced in liquid form via electrolysis and subsequently cast into its first solid form (smelt & cast rule). For the secondary production route, origin shall be determined based on the country of smelt for the primary input and the country of most recent cast for the scrap input.
ev.justification: For steel, the current definition using Regulation (EU) No 2013/952 cannot apply, as its ‘last substantial transformation’ rule would undermine the objective by allowing third-country steel to gain Union origin status through minor downstream processing. Such a loophole would risk diverting decarbonisation investments away from Europe and rewarding imports of partly finished products instead of supporting genuine EU -based production. A steel melt and pour requirement is necessary as an additional criterion in Article 7 to ensure that the objectives of the IAA are being met i.e. growing industry within the EU, securing EU resilience, strategic autonomy, economic security and public order. In particular, the Union Origin definition of Article 7 is relevant in the context of the Low-Carbon Steel Credit made in the EU under the CO2 standards of cars and vans. Therefore, it is about strengthening the automotive value-chain in the EU. Referencing the “melt and pour” definition adopted in Regulation EU 2025/0726 ensures regulatory coherence. Moreover, it makes sure that the major steelmaking processes and decarbonisation takes place in the EU, and therefore ensures a lead market demand that recognises EU investments. Article 7.2 refers to Products and Components, which confirms the intention to cover all made of steel products.

ev.amended: 2a.The Commission shall review the definition of the last substantial transformation referred in Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council for products and components covered by this Chapter with the aim of including a minimum 50% of Union added value for those products and components with the aim to avoid circumvention of the rules of origin.

2a.The Commission shall review the definition of the last substantial transformation referred in Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council for products and components covered by this Chapter with the aim of including a minimum 50% of Union added value for those products and components with the aim to avoid circumvention of the rules of origin.

2a.The Commission shall review the definition of the last substantial transformation referred in Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council for products and components covered by this Chapter with the aim of including a minimum 50% of Union added value for those products and components with the aim to avoid circumvention of the rules of origin.

2a.The Union origin and low-carbon requirements laid down in this Chapter shall only apply at the point of the procurement procedure or awarding of support under Articles 11 and 12. They shall not restrict the lawful use of spare parts and components that do not comply with the relevant Union origin and low-carbon requirements during the vehicle's or product's lifetime.

2a.The Union origin requirements referred to in this Chapter should not preclude contracting authorities and contracting entities in Ireland from allowing tenders submitted by economic operators established in the North of Ireland to access procurement procedures, in recognition of the all-island dimension of Ireland's economy.

2a.The Commission shall review the definition of the last substantial transformation referred in Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council for products and components covered by this Regulation with the aim to avoid circumvention of the rules of origin.

2a.For steel products, steel components and products containing steel, only steel originally melted and poured within the Union shall qualify as content of Union origin. Subsequent processing or transformation shall not alter the origin of the steel for the purposes of this Chapter.

2a.The Commission shall ensure that compliance mechanisms related to Union origin requirements remain proportionate to the size, resources and administrative capacity of SMEs. Standardised declaration templates and digital tools should be made available to facilitate compliance.

2a.By way of derogation from paragraph 2, for steel products, components and assembled final products containing steel only steel that has been originally melted and poured in the Union, in accordance with Regulation 2026/1384, shall qualify as of Union origin.
ev.justification: Union Custom code referred to in par. 2, the origin of a product is determined based on the last substantial transformation carried out in the Union. For steel products, Union origin may therefore be conferred on imported semi-finished products even though the upstream carbon intensive production processes have taken place outside the Union. Art. 7 must clearly stipulate that only steel originally melted and poured in the Union can qualify as Union origin.

ev.amended: 2a.In evaluating compliance with Union origin requirements, specific account shall be taken of the structural constraints faced by small island Member States, including reliance on imported raw materials and intermediate inputs required for local manufacturing.
ev.justification: Origin-verification rules should account for the higher costs faced by small island economies. While the EU-wide estimate is around EUR 19 per resident, the indicative additional cost for these economies is EUR 64–94 per resident. They rely heavily on imported materials and technology, but benefit less directly from the manufacturing gains included in the Commission’s assessment. The rules should reflect this imbalance to avoid putting them at a disadvantage in the single market.

ev.amended: 2a.Where the above conditions are not met, the Commission, Member State, contracting authority or contracting entity shall exclude the third country, or the economic operator operating in that third country, from benefitting from this regulation.

2a.For steel products and components containing steel, only steel originally melted and pour within the Union, on the basis of the "melt and pour" principle as defined under the Regulation (EU) 2026/1384, shall qualify as being of Union origin.

2a.For steel products, components and assembled final products containing steel, only steel that has been originally melted and poured within the Union, in accordance with Regulation (EU 2026/1384), shall qualify as being of Union origin.
ev.justification: For steel, the current definition using Regulation (EU) No 2013/952 cannot apply, as its ‘last substantial transformation’ rule would undermine the objective by allowing third-country steel to gain Union origin status through minor downstream processing. Such a loophole would risk diverting decarbonisation investments away from Europe and rewarding imports of partly finished products instead of supporting genuine EU -based production. The “melt and pour” criteria adopted in Regulation EU 2025/0726 ensures that the major steelmaking processes and decarbonisation takes place in the EU, and therefore ensures a lead market demand that recognises EU investments.

ev.amended: 2a.For steel products and components containing steel, only steel originally melted and poured within the Union shall qualify as Union origin product.

2b.Pending the development and implementation of more advanced frameworks for political and economic association with the Union, the competent authorities and the Commission shall endeavour to grant the most favourable treatment and the most flexible application of the provisions of this Chapter to products, services and investments originating in third countries which already have associations or trade agreements with the Union, which are part of a customs union with the Union or which belong to the European Economic Area. That treatment shall apply in particular during the transitional period prior to the entry into force of the acts referred to in this Article, in order to preserve the economic integration and continuity of strategic value chains with those partners.

2b.Where severe supply chain disruptions, market availability limits, or disproportionate compliance costs impact small island economies, Member States may grant temporary derogations or apply flexible origin-calculation rules to ensure local industries are not excluded from enabling measures under this Chapter.
ev.justification: Small manufacturers in island economies should not lose access to industrial support because supply disruptions, limited suppliers or high transport costs make origin requirements harder to meet. Temporary derogations or flexible origin calculations would protect local production and investment where compliance is excessively costly or impractical. Such measures would apply only where objectively justified, for as long as necessary, without undermining the EU’s origin objectives.

ev.amended: 2b.For the purposes of paragraph 2, a tyre shall be considered to be of EU origin where it has been vulcanised in the Union. A retreaded tyre shall be considered to be of EU origin when the retreading, including the vulcanisation of the new tread, has been carried out in the Union.
ev.justification: Vulcanisation is the industrial process that gives the tyre its essential characteristics. Making this the criterion for origin – in accordance with the rules based on sufficient processing used in trade agreements – provides a workable, verifiable and easily monitored rule, given that some raw materials, such as natural rubber, cannot be produced within the Union.

ev.amended: 2b.Where that review identifies a risk of circumvention or finds that the applicable rules do not ensure genuine value creation within the Union for specific products or components, the Commission shall take appropriate action in accordance with the relevant provisions of Regulation (EU) No 2026/2108.

2b.By way of derogation from any delegated acts adopted based on paragraph 2b, with respect to the Union origin requirements referred to in Article 12, content of Union origin refers to content originating in the Union pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article.
2b.The Union origin conditions applicable to products and components under this Regulation shall be assessed on the basis of the cumulative conditions laid down in paragraph 2a.
2b.For the purposes of this Regulation, metal products shall be deemed to originate in the Union where they have been melted and cast in the Union.
ev.justification: For the metal sector, the mandatory introduction of a “melted and poured” requirement is essential to prevent any circumvention of the rules of origin, as steelmaking constitutes the central and defining stage of the production process from both an industrial and an environmental perspective.

ev.amended:
2c.By way of exception, critical raw materials, industrial resources and essential inputs for the value chains covered by this Regulation that originate in an eligible overseas country or territory within the meaning of Article 3, point 40b, shall be treated as content of Union origin. The origin of those materials, resources and inputs shall be determined in accordance with the rules applicable under Council Decision (EU) 2021/1764.
This treatment shall be subject to the condition that their extraction, processing or production complies with appropriate requirements relating to the protection of biodiversity, water management, pollution prevention, waste treatment and environmental traceability.
It shall be strictly limited to the materials, resources and inputs referred to in the first subparagraph and shall not confer on the products concerned non-preferential Union origin within the meaning of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013.

2c.When assessing countries’ applications under the ‘opt-in’ procedure, the Commission shall give priority to European countries, in line with the European dimension of the Union as reflected in the Treaties, in particular Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, and taking into account the extent to which the countries concerned are integrated into the Union’s value chains. This applies in particular to the countries of the European Economic Area and the European Free Trade Association, the United Kingdom and the candidate countries with which accession negotiations are actively being conducted. For candidate countries, eligibility for this priority is subject to a rate of alignment in excess of at least 80 % with declarations and decisions relating to the Common Foreign and Security Policy, as indicated in the Commission’s latest annual report on enlargement.
ev.justification: The transition from automatic equivalence to recognition on request must not penalise the European partners that are most closely integrated into the internal market. This amendment enshrines in the enacting terms the objective of progressive integration of candidate countries into the Union’s value chains, as set out in recital 17. It establishes a hierarchy based on Article 49 TEU and on an objective criterion of economic integration.

ev.amended: 2c.When applying paragraph 2b, the Commission shall give priority to European countries, in line with the European dimension of the Union as reflected in the Treaties, in particular Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, and if necessary for taking into account the integration of those countries in Union value chains, in particular the countries of the EEA, EFTA and the United Kingdom.

2c.When applying paragraph 2b, the Commission shall give priority to European countries, in line with the European dimension of the Union as reflected in the Treaties, in particular Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, and if necessary for taking into account the integration of those countries in Union value chains, in particular the countries of the EEA, EFTA and the United Kingdom.

2c.Steel products and components shall be considered to be of Union origin where the steel used in their manufacture has been originally melted and poured within the Union, in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2026/1384, Regulation (EU) 2026/1963 and any implementing, delegated or other acts adopted pursuant to those regulations.

2c.By way of derogation from any delegated acts adopted based on paragraph 2b, with respect to the Union origin requirements referred to in Article 12, content of Union origin refers to content originating in the Union pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article.

2c.By way of derogation from any delegated acts adopted based on paragraph 2b, with respect to the Union origin requirements referred to in Article 12, content of Union origin refers to content originating in the Union pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article.

2d.The Commission shall annually publish a report and present it to the European Parliament and Council about the implementation of this Article. This report shall provide for an analysis of the market situation, and an overview of their activities regarding adoption or non-adoption of delegated acts.
The report shall also assess whether further conditionalities, in particular with regard to climate, environmental and social standards, are needed to ensure a level playing-field.
The European Parliament through its competent committees may provide an opinion on the report by the Commission to outline its position.

2d.When applying paragraph 2b, the Commission shall give priority to European countries, in line with the European dimension of the Union as reflected in the Treaties, in particular Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, and if necessary for taking into account the integration of those countries in Union value chains, in particular the countries of the EEA, EFTA and the United Kingdom.

Article 7a
Anti-circumvention of Union origin
1. Content originating from partner countries shall not be considered to be of Union origin, where circumvention exists. Circumvention exists where either of the following applies:
(a) the content is produced by an economic operator owned or controlled by a natural or legal person from a third country which holds more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in the sector concerned;
(b) more than 50% of the value of the parts of the product originates in a third country which holds more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in the sector concerned.
Ownership and control shall be assessed at the level of the beneficial owner at the end of the ownership chain, including where exercised indirectly through any person or undertaking acting on behalf of or at the direction of that owner. Control shall be presumed where such persons hold, individually or collectively, 25% or more of the share capital or voting rights of the operator concerned, or of the assets used to produce the content.
2. An economic operator offering content as equivalent to Union origin shall carry out a self-assessment to determine whether the content is subject to circumvention. On that basis it shall submit a self-declaration. The Commission shall adopt implementing acts laying down the standard form of that declaration, in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 31(2).
3. Where circumvention by an economic operator is established on a second or any subsequent occasion within three years, that economic operator and any undertaking controlled by the same beneficial owner shall be excluded from any procedure or support covered by this Regulation for a period of between one and three years.
ev.justification: Partner content must not become a back door around the origin rules. Think of a battery plant in a partner country, owned by a company from a country that dominates global production. Companies offering partner content check this themselves in one standard form. A company caught twice with a false declaration within three years is excluded for one to three years. The 50% threshold is the same single-country cap the Commission already uses in the NZIA.

ev.amended:
Article 7a
Economic security
1. The strategic sectors and technologies covered by this Regulation are essential for protecting the Union’s economic security and safeguarding its essential security interests within the meaning of Article XXI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and Article III of the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement.
2. For the purposes of public procurement procedures, public support schemes, auctions and other forms of public intervention falling within the scope of this Regulation, and in relation to products, components or technologies, the Union hereby invokes the security exceptions referred to in paragraph 1.
3. In respect of the procedures and forms of intervention referred to in paragraph 2, content originating in third countries shall not be regarded as being of Union origin and shall not be treated as content of Union origin for the purposes of this Regulation. By way of an exception, critical raw materials, industrial resources and strategic inputs originating in an overseas country or territory listed in Annex II to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union may be treated as provided for in Article 7(2c), subject to the conditions laid down in that provision.
4. Notification of the invocation of the security exceptions referred to in paragraph 2 shall be provided to the relevant WTO bodies in accordance with the applicable procedures. The recitals to this Regulation set out the security justification for each sector and technology.

Article 7a
Union origin for softwares
For the purposes of this Regulation, where a Union origin requirement applies to software which is not subject to the rules for determining the non-preferential origin of goods under Regulation (EU) No 2026/2108, the Union origin of that software shall be determined on the basis of the place where the principal development activities resulting in the essential characteristics and functionalities of the software are carried out.
In determining whether software is of Union origin, account shall be taken, in particular, of the place where the principal software architecture, development, programming, testing, validation and integration activities are carried out and of the share of the value of those activities generated within the Union.
The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 30 to supplement this Regulation by establishing the methodology and criteria for determining the Union origin of software pursuant to this paragraph, including rules concerning software developed in more than one country and rules necessary to prevent circumvention.

Article 7b
Anticircumvention of Union origin equivalence
Where there is sufficient evidence that the treatment as Union origin provided for in Article 8 or 9 is being obtained through practices that circumvent the conditions or objectives underlying that treatment, the Commission may initiate an investigation with a view to withdrawing or suspending that treatment in respect of the third country, product or economic operator concerned.
For the purposes of this Article, circumvention means a change in the pattern of trade or production stemming from a practice, process or operation for which there is insufficient due cause or economic justification other than obtaining the treatment provided for in Article 8 or 9, including in particular:
(a) the assembly or completion, in a third country benefiting from that treatment, of parts or components originating in other third countries, where the processing or working carried out is minor having regard to the nature and value of the parts or components concerned; or
(b) the relocation or establishment in a third country benefiting from that treatment of processing, assembly or manufacturing operations which generate only limited local value creation and do not reflect genuine manufacturing capacity.
The Commission may initiate an investigation on its own initiative or following a substantiated request from a Member State, a contracting authority or representatives of Union industry. The Commission shall inform the third country and the economic operators concerned of the initiation of the investigation and shall provide them with an opportunity to submit relevant information. The investigation shall be concluded within nine months of its initiation.
Where the Commission determines that circumvention has taken place, it shall, by means of an implementing act adopted in accordance with Article [XX], withdraw or suspend the treatment provided for in Article 8 or 9 in respect of the products or economic operators concerned or, where the circumvention is systemic and cannot effectively be addressed through measures limited to individual products or economic operators, in respect of the third country concerned. Any measure adopted pursuant to this paragraph shall be proportionate to the circumvention identified.

Article7b
Monitoring of circumvention
1. The Commission shall monitor the following indicators for each partner country:
(a) imports into the Union from that partner country, compared with that country's imports of components and inputs from a third country which holds more than 40% of global manufacturing capacity in the sector concerned, and with the share of its production exported to the Union;
(b) foreign direct investment from such a third country in production facilities or warehouses in that partner country;
(c) the participation of economic operators from that partner country in procurement procedures and support schemes covered by this Regulation.
Where those indicators point to a risk of circumvention, the Commission shall, on its own initiative or at the request of a Member State, issue an early warning for a product category and country.
2. The Commission shall investigate the accuracy of a self-declaration following an early warning or a substantiated request from a Member State, and may do so on its own initiative. Member States, contracting authorities, contracting entities and representative organisations of the sectors concerned may submit to the Commission any relevant evidence. The Commission shall conclude the investigation within nine months and, where the self-declaration is found to be false, establish circumvention by decision.
3. Where early warnings or established cases of circumvention recur in respect of a partner country, the Commission shall assess whether that country still meets the criteria for partner country status and shall, where appropriate, exclude it in accordance with Article 7.
ev.justification: The Commission tracks a few simple indicators per partner country: imports compared with the partner's own imports of parts and its export share, investment from dominant third countries, and participation in Union tenders and schemes. Where these point to a risk, it must issue an early warning and investigate. An investigation takes at most nine months. If cases keep recurring, the partner country can lose its status.

ev.justification: The legislation should make clear that appropriate checks must be carried out and that failure to comply with customs arrangements may result in a product being denied European-origin status. There is the need to ensure that the provisions of the Act concerning the recognition of goods from third countries with which the EU has concluded a free trade agreement or customs union, as Union-origin products, do not create incentives for nearshoring and offshoring policies that could negatively affect European industry.

However, the automatic application of content equivalence to Union origin should not lead to entrenched strategic dependencies or to situations where European producers are at a disadvantage compared to third-country operators. ev.amended: 1.With respect to the Union origin requirements referred to in Article 11, content originating in third countries with which the Union has concluded an agreement establishing a free trade area or a customs union, or that are parties to the Agreement on Government Procurement, where relevant obligations of the Union exist under that agreement, as well as content originating in other trusted partner countries where reciprocity, security of supply and resilient integration into Union value chains are demonstrated, shall be deemed to be of Union origin.
ev.justification: Malta relies heavily on diversified international supply chains for access to raw materials, components, equipment and technologies that are not produced domestically or are not available in sufficient quantities within the Union. A narrowly defined “Made in Europe” approach could therefore increase costs, restrict supplier choice and expose smaller, import-dependent Member States to supply disruptions, without necessarily delivering a proportionate increase in Union industrial capacity. The amendment preserves the objective of strengthening European production and strategic resilience while recognising the contribution of trusted partner countries. Treating qualifying partner content as equivalent to Union origin would reflect the operational reality of modern manufacturing, in which final products frequently incorporate inputs sourced across closely interconnected and rules-based supply networks. It would also help European manufacturers remain competitive by ensuring continued access to specialised inputs, critical components and technologies that cannot readily be substituted in the short or medium term. For Malta, this flexibility is particularly important to safeguard the affordability and timely delivery of public and private investment projects, preserve effective competition and avoid disproportionate disadvantages arising from geographic insularity, limited domestic production and a small internal market. Eligibility should nevertheless be based on transparent criteria and regularly reviewed. This balanced “Made with Europe” approach would strengthen Europe’s industrial base through cooperation with reliable partners, diversify external dependencies and reduce strategic vulnerabilities, while ensuring that European preference does not become an overly restrictive instrument that undermines competitiveness, investment or supply-chain resilience

ev.amended: 1.With respect to the Union origin requirements referred to in Article 11, content originating in the European Union Member States, and the EEA/EFTA States, shall be deemed to be of Union origin.
ev.justification: Over 75% of EU steel imports come from freetradeagreement countries, the rule could allow products from nearly 80 countries to qualify as ‘Made in EU.’ Having such a broad eligibility to access lead markets will weaken demand for EU produced low-carbon steel, and perversely use public funds to incentivise imports and weaken the investment case within the EU. The current definition would also allow producers from third countries, e.g. China, to maintain market access by shifting investment to partner countries qualifying under EU trade arrangements (e.g. Morocco, Turkey or Serbia), without strengthening European industrial capacity. For this reason, the definition of “Union origin” should be limited to production within the EU, the European Economic Area and EFTA countries. Limiting eligibility for Public Procurement lead markets is required in order to meet the objectives of the IAA and is justified under the following WTO exceptions: - GPA: Article III.2(a) – public order; - GATT: the recitals point to Article XX(j) (critical shortages), Article XXI (essential security interests) and/or Article XX(a) (public morals linked to public order).

1a.By way of derogation from Article 11(1), a legal entity established in the Union and controlled by an entity established in a third country which has not concluded an international agreement referred to in Article 11(1) shall not be excluded where it provides the contracting authority or contracting entity with evidence of guarantees approved in accordance with the national procedures of the Member State in which it is established, including, where applicable, appropriate mitigation measures pursuant to screening within the meaning of Article 2, point (3), of Regulation (EU) 2019/452.
The guarantees referred to in the second paragraph shall demonstrate that the economic operator:
a) forms part of a group listed on a recognised and regulated European stock exchange, or can otherwise demonstrate that it meets equivalent corporate governance requirements;
b) has its headquarters within the Union; a
c) and has more than 50% of its global manufacturing capacity and workforce within the Union.
For the purposes of points a) to c), the guarantees shall be based on information relating to the preceding financial year. The contracting authority or contracting entity shall verify that the economic operator has provided evidence of guarantees approved in accordance with the second paragraph. Where the economic operator is awarded a contract, it shall provide annual confirmation throughout the duration of the contract that the criteria set out in points a) to c) continue to be fulfilled.

1a.Access to public procurement, public support, auctions, fast-track procedures and other benefits under this Regulation shall be conditional upon compliance with applicable labour and social legislation, collective agreements, occupational health and safety principles, and commitments on high-quality and stable jobs. Beneficiaries shall respect freedom of association, the right to collective bargaining, and the right to information and consultation with workers’ representatives.

1a.The provisions set out in this regulation shall apply only to public procurement procedures with an estimated value, net of value added tax, at or above the relevant threshold set out in Article 4 of Directive 2014/24/EU, Article 15 of Directive 2014/25/EU or Article 8 of Directive 2014/23/EU, as applicable, as those thresholds are revised from time to time in accordance with those Directives.

1a.For the purposes of public procurement procedures, public support schemes, auctions and other forms of public intervention falling within the scope of this Regulation, and in relation to products, components or technologies, the Union hereby invokes the security exceptions referred to in paragraph 1.

1a.The requirements laid down in Part I of Annex II shall not apply to public procurement procedures concerning civil energy infrastructure or civil water and wastewater infrastructure. This paragraph shall be without prejudice to the requirements laid down in Regulation (EU) 2024/1735.

1a.This Article shall apply only to public procurement procedures with an estimated value reaching or exceeding an amount three times the relevant threshold referred to in Directive 2014/23/EU, Directive 2014/24/EU or Directive 2014/25/EU, as applicable.
ev.justification: Without a separate threshold, the requirements for public procurement set out in the IAA would cover all procurement procedures falling within regular thresholds of relevant EU legislation. The amendment aims to ensure proportionality and avoiding undue burden on on the public sector in the case of smaller projects by keeping only larger procurement procedures in scope. The threshold is set as "three times" rather than a fixed amount, to account for revisions of existing thresholds in light of inflation etc.

ev.amended: 1a.By way of derogation from paragraph 1, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall not exclude economic operators referred to in paragraph 1 if they hold a valid certificate of eligibility issued in accordance with paragraph 1b.

1b.By way of derogation from Article 11(1), a legal entity established in the Union and controlled by an entity established in a third country which has not concluded an international agreement referred to in Article 11(1), shall not be excluded where it provides the contracting authority with evidence of guarantees approved in accordance with the national procedures of the Member State in which it is established, such as adequate measures pursuant to screening.
The guarantees referred to in the second paragraph shall provide sufficient assurances that, notwithstanding the control exercised over the legal entity, the legal entity has the operational and managerial autonomy necessary to perform the contract, in particular as regards security of supply and continuity of production.

1b.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall exclude from public procurement procedures tenders relating to products that cannot demonstrate effective compliance with the health, environmental and safety standards applicable in the Union, in particular under Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 concerning the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals (REACH), Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 and Regulation (EU) 2023/988 on general product safety. The burden of proof regarding such compliance shall lie with the economic operator. A sworn statement shall not be sufficient where the contracting authority or contracting entity has established that objective doubt exists.

1c.The economic operator shall inform the Investment Authority which issued the certificate without delay of any change liable to affect compliance with the conditions laid down in paragraph 1b. The Investment Authority may carry out checks at any time during the period of validity of the certificate, in particular as regards changes in control, registered office or manufacturing activities in the Union, and shall do so where it has reasons to believe that the conditions laid down in paragraph 1b are no longer met or at the request of the Commission. It shall withdraw the certificate where the economic operator no longer meets the conditions laid down in paragraph 1b or where the certificate was issued on the basis of incorrect or misleading information. The Commission may request the withdrawal of a certificate. The withdrawal shall be recorded without delay in the register referred to in paragraph 1b.

ev.original: 2.For public procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements and low-carbon requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 8 and 10.
ev.amended: 2.For public procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements and low-carbon requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 8 and 10. Union origin requirements shall be implemented on a level playing field between economic operators in all Member States and may not lead to discrimination of products or components originating in a specific Member State. Contracting authorities shall take into account, insofar as possible, the contribution of public procurement procedures to the development of manufacturing capacities and value chains in Member States and regions with a lower level of industrial development.
ev.justification: Although the Regulation aims to strengthen the Union’s industrial capacity, a European procurement mechanism may in practice end up favouring already very large manufacturers if we do not take care to ensure access for all Member States. The Commission proposal itself justifies the IAA by strengthening the European industrial base and resilience.

ev.original: 2.For public procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements and low-carbon requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 8 and 10.
ev.amended: 2.For public procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements in conjunction with the requirement for the economic operator and the manufacturer of the products referred to in Annex II to have a fixed establishment within the European Union territory and low-carbon requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 7, 10 and 10a. The base tender price is determined by taking market prices for products of Union Origin as a reference parameter.
ev.justification: The amendment raises public procurement standards by imposing, in addition to EU origin requirements and low carbon criteria, a stable organization within the European territory for operators and producers, with reference to the sectors listed in Annex II. The aim is to strengthen strategic autonomy, understood as the European Union's capacity to control critical supply chain nodes, reduce excessive dependencies, and protect European companies from the pressure of a globalized market with fewer constraints. Setting the tender base price on market prices of products of European origin ('Union origin') ensures fair competition, enhancing quality and sustainability over the lowest price alone."

ev.original: 2.For public procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements and low-carbon requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 8 and 10.
ev.amended: 2.For public procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements and low-carbon requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 8 and 10. In applying those requirements, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall preserve effective competition and value for money and shall ensure that the requirements do not artificially restrict the number of eligible economic operators or favour a specific economic operator.
ev.justification: Although the Commission proposal recognises effective competition and value for money in its recitals, those principles should also appear expressly in the operative provisions in order to have clear practical effect when contracting authorities apply Union-origin and low-carbon requirements. Incorporating these safeguards into Article 11(2) would provide a clear legal basis to design proportionate tender conditions, assess market availability and avoid requirements that unnecessarily narrow the pool of eligible suppliers. It would help prevent procurement specifications from being formulated or applied in a manner that directly or indirectly favours a particular economic operator, technology, product or national market structure. This is especially important in smaller and more concentrated markets such as Malta, where only a limited number of suppliers may be able to satisfy strict origin or low-carbon conditions and where the exclusion of even a few operators can materially weaken competition, increase prices and delay essential public projects. It would require objectives to be pursued in a manner consistent with equal treatment, non-discrimination, proportionality, transparency and sound financial management. The amendment would also reduce legal uncertainty and the risk of procurement challenges by making clear that authorities must document how competition and value for money were preserved when preparing tender specifications and evaluating offers. This balanced approach would support European industrial capacity while ensuring that public purchasers retain access to sufficiently competitive markets, obtain sustainable outcomes over the full contract lifecycle and use public funds responsibly

2a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall exclude economic operators from access to procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III where such operators including their subcontractors do not comply with applicable obligations in the fields of social and labour law established by Union law, national law, collective agreements, or by the fundamental ILO conventions.
Tender documents shall, where linked to the subject matter of the contract and proportionate, include social and labour-related contract-performance conditions, including measures relating to skills, apprenticeship and vocational training opportunities, and the creation and maintenance of quality jobs. Where the performance of the contract involves subcontracting, the applicable social and employment-related obligations and contract-performance conditions shall apply, where relevant and proportionate, throughout the relevant subcontracting chain.

2a.By way of derogation from paragraph 2, where a public procurement procedure referred to in Part I of Annex II or Part I of Annex III concerns the conclusion of a framework agreement with several economic operators, the Union origin requirements shall be deemed to be fulfilled where at least 50% of the total value or volume of products, services or works awarded over the duration of the framework agreement complies with the requirements laid down therein in accordance with Articles 7 and 8. Within that limit, contracting authorities and contracting entities may award specific contracts among the economic operators party to the framework agreement in a manner that maintains operational flexibility and secures access to essential technologies.

2a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall, at any time during the procedure, exclude economic operators from participation in a procurement procedure referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III where any of the mandatory grounds for exclusion laid down in Article 25 of [Proposal for Public Procurement Act] apply.
Contracting authorities and contracting entities may exclude economic operators from those procedures where any of the optional grounds for exclusion laid down in Article 26 of [Proposal for Public Procurement Act] apply.

2a.The application of paragraph 2 shall not require the use of a particular construction material where another material or combination of materials meets the relevant functional, safety and environmental requirements. Where appropriate, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall formulate technical specifications in terms of performance or functional requirements. The applicable requirements in Annex II shall continue to apply to the covered products actually used in the contract.
ev.justification: The Regulation should not lock public construction into particular materials or disadvantage innovative, sustainable alternatives. The amendment preserves the requirements for covered products while enabling performance-based procurement.

ev.amended: 2a.By way of derogation from paragraph 2, where a public procurement procedure referred to in Part I of Annex II or Part I of Annex III concerns the conclusion of a framework agreement with several economic operators, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall ensure that at least 50% of the economic operators party to the framework agreement supply products, services or works that comply with the Union origin requirements laid down therein in accordance with Article 7.
ev.justification: Introducing necessary operational flexibility for contracting authorities and entities, particularly utilities, ensuring they can fulfil their public service obligations without supply chain disruptions. Shifting the European preference criteria in multi-supplier framework agreements from a strict volume-based threshold to a 50 per cent supplier-based threshold acknowledges that current Union manufacturing capacity is insufficient in critical sectors, such as solar photovoltaics and electrical transformers. This adjustment guarantees a strong lead market for European industry while allowing public buyers to award specific contracts to non-Union suppliers when domestic alternatives are constrained or not currently available.

ev.amended: 2a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall exclude economic operators from access to procurement procedures referred to in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III where such operators do not comply with applicable obligations in the fields of social and labour law established by Union law, national law, collective agreements, or by the fundamental ILO conventions.

2a.For public procurement procedures referred to in [part I of Annex IV new], contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the Union origin requirements laid down therein in accordance with Article 8.

2c.At the contract award stage, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply a weighted criterion, accounting for between 15 % and 20 % of the total assessment, to reward content of Union origin exceeding the minimum threshold stated in paragraph 2.

ev.justification: The exclusion of the tenderer according to par 1 shall be facultative in those cases as well. But most importantly – the wording of the derogations will be extremely confusing in practice. The proposed derogation appears to transplant elements from the PP directive on the use of the negotiated procedure without prior publication, which pursue a different regulatory purpose - justifying the absence of competition. Furthermore, the proposal uses the PP directives imprecisely (p.e. what is a suitable tender ? see Art 32(2)(a) of the PP Dir). This will most likely create interpretative and application difficulties in practice. A more coherent solution would be to provide that this Article does not apply where the contract is awarded in a negotiated procedure without prior publication, besides allowing the proposed derogations.

Estimated cost differences exceeding 15%, based on objective and transparent data, may be presumed by contracting authorities and contracting entities to be disproportionate.
ev.justification: A 25% cost differential is excessively high for public procurement. In high-value infrastructure, energy, transport, digital and strategic manufacturing projects, even a considerably smaller percentage increase may translate into significant additional expenditure for public budgets and reduce the resources available for other essential services or investments. A 15% benchmark would provide a more realistic, while still allowing authorities to accept a higher-priced compliant offer where this is objectively justified. The lower threshold would be particularly important for Malta, where the available supplier base is narrower, transport and logistics costs are structurally higher, and origin requirements may have a stronger effect on tender prices than in larger continental markets. Without an effective safeguard, contracting authorities could face reduced competition, fewer eligible bids, delayed procedures or the cancellation and downsizing of necessary projects. The 15% presumption would not create an automatic exemption or prevent the application of Union-origin requirements. Rather, it would establish a clearer evidentiary benchmark based on objective and transparent data, enabling authorities to assess the total financial impact of those requirements in a proportionate manner. Authorities should remain able to consider the full lifecycle cost of the contract, instead of relying solely on the initial purchase price. This approach would ensure that procurement remains competitive, fiscally responsible and capable of delivering genuine value for money. It would also reduce the risk that an excessively permissive cost threshold indirectly favours a limited group of suppliers, imposes disproportionate burdens on smaller public administrations or weakens public acceptance of the Union’s industrial policy objectives through avoidable cost increases

(cb)their application would lead to a significant distortion of competition in downstream markets in which private undertakings are competing with a contracting entity. A significant distortion of competition with private undertakings shall be presumed where private undertakings hold a market share in downstream markets of more than 40% in the relevant market and any of the following criteria apply
(i) compliance with the requirements would increase the contracting entity’s costs by more than 10% compared to those incurred by its private competitors; or
(ii) a market assessment demonstrates that the requirements are likely to reduce the number of suitable economic operators by more than 30%.
ev.justification: If public undertakings (“contracting entities”) compete with private undertakings in downstream markets, such as electricity generation and sales, mandatory EU sourcing requirements for components or primary goods (e.g. steel or concrete) may result in significant additional costs for public undertakings. In competitive markets, public undertakings may be unable to pass these additional costs on to consumers and could consequently be placed at a competitive disadvantage or ultimately forced out of the market. An upper cost threshold of 25%, or even 40%, as currently foreseen is therefore too high to ensure that public undertakings can remain competitive with private undertakings. A market-distortion opt-out is consequently necessary.

ev.amended: (cb)the contracting authority, on the basis of a prior market consultation or of the tenders received, that products complying with the requirements are not available, or not available in sufficient quantities, on the market of the Member State concerned or of neighbouring Member States within delivery times and at transport costs compatible with the execution of the contract, in particular where no production of the relevant product exists in that Member State.

(cb)their application would result in a material delay to the implementation of the project, or would otherwise threaten the security of supply in the Union of the products in question, in particular where this would adversely affect system reliability or the timely delivery of critical infrastructure.

The derogation reflects the security exceptions in Union procurement law, such as Article 15 of Directive 2014/24/EU and Article 24 of Directive 2014/25/EU, and in trade agreements.

ev.amended: (cc)their application would prevent the contracting authority or contracting entity to comply with safety, security and/or cybersecurity requirements.

3a.In the outermost regions referred to in Article 349 TFEU and the overseas countries and territories referred to in Article 355(2) TFEU, the contracting authorities and contracting entities may also decide to not apply, whether in full or in part, the Union origin requirements laid down in Annexes II and III where their application would, on account of remoteness, insularity or transport costs, result in cost differences or delays exceeding the thresholds set by the Member State concerned. Each Member State shall set these thresholds, differentiated or otherwise, depending on the territory and product category. This power may not be exercised where a compliant tender relies on production carried out in the outermost region or overseas country or territory concerned.

3a.In applying the requirements set out in this Article in the outermost regions referred to in Article 349 TFEU, the Member States concerned may take into account the permanent structural constraints of those regions and may adapt the application of those requirements accordingly, with a view to supporting local production capacity. Any such adaptation shall be consistent with the specific measures adopted on the basis of Article 349 TFEU to support those regions, in particular the schemes of differentiated taxation and the regional operating aid applicable to them, and shall comply with the applicable Union public procurement framework.
ev.justification: The outermost regions form part of the Union customs territory and their production already qualifies as Union origin. Support for their local production is channelled, under Article 349 TFEU, through dedicated instruments such as differentiated taxation and regional operating aid. This enabling provision ensures that those regions are taken into account in the procurement provisions of this Regulation and leaves it to the Member State concerned to adapt the application of the requirements in a manner consistent with those instruments, without creating a separate or binding local-content regime.

ev.amended: 3a.The decision not to apply the requirements set out in Annexes II and III pursuant to points (a), (b) or (c) shall be duly justified and documented in writing by the contracting authority or contracting entity. (cc) their application would materially restrict security of supply or effective competition because compliant products are unavailable in sufficient quantities or within reasonable delivery times, taking into account the specific geographic, insular, peripheral or highly import-dependent characteristics of the market concerned.

3a.This Article shall be without prejudice to shorter time limits laid down in national law. ev.justification: Shorter national time limits should be preserved, in line with Regulations (EU) 2024/1735 and (EU) 2024/1252. Annual reporting and a public comparative overview will ensure that the acceleration of permitting is effectively implemented in all Member States.

ev.amended: 3b.In the outermost regions referred to in Article 349 TFEU and the overseas countries and territories referred to in Article 355(2) TFEU, the contracting authorities and contracting entities may also decide to not apply, whether in full or in part, the Union origin requirements laid down in Annexes II and III where their application would, on account of remoteness, insularity or transport costs, result in cost differences or delays exceeding the thresholds set by the Member State concerned. ev.original: 4.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall require economic operators supplying products or services to submit a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Article.

ev.original: 4.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall require economic operators supplying products or services to submit a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Article.
ev.amended: 4.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall require economic operators supplying products or services to submit a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Article. They shall accept relevant documentation already issued or verified under Union law and shall not require duplicate certification of the same facts. ev.original: 4.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall require economic operators supplying products or services to submit a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Article.
ev.amended: 4.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall require economic operators supplying products or services to submit a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Article. Any subsequent review of the aforementioned documents of the successful bidder will be conducted by the European Commission. Contractors may rely on the accuracy of information and documentation provided to them by manufacturers, suppliers, or other third parties. They shall not be liable for incorrect or incomplete information provided by third parties, provided that they were neither aware of the inaccuracy nor should have been aware of it had they exercised due diligence.
ev.justification: Verifying self-declarations concerning the low-carbon production of products, as well as determining whether an economic operator fulfils the requirement of Union origin, generally falls outside the expertise and capabilities of public contracting authorities. The verification of such self-declarations should therefore be carried out by, or at a minimum supported by, the European Commission. Economic operators generally lack both the legal and practical means to independently verify the accuracy of information provided by manufacturers or other supporting documentation. Strict liability for inaccurate information provided by third parties would create significant legal uncertainty and disproportionate risks for contractors. Therefore, it needs to be ensured that economic operators may rely on information provided by their suppliers and that they are liable only where they knew that the information was inaccurate or ignored obvious inconsistencies.

ev.original: 4.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall require economic operators supplying products or services to submit a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Article.

Where there are justified grounds to carry out risk-based checks on the accuracy of the self-declarations, contracting authorities and contracting entities may require the economic operator to provide supporting documents to substantiate that self-declaration, in accordance with Directive 2014/23/EU, 2014/24/EU or 2014/25/EU.
