(a)Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall not require small volume manufacturers, as defined in Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/631, with a production site established and owned within the Union before the publication of the proposal for this Regulation, including R&D facilities, full engineering capabilities and a highly skilled workforce, to comply with the requirements set out in Annexes II and III.
ev.justification: Small volume manufacturers established in the Union face structural constraints in sourcing Union-origin components and do not have the same negotiating power as large-volume manufacturers. Specific flexibility is therefore necessary to preserve their manufacturing, R&D and engineering capabilities in Europe, while recognising their contribution to the Union’s industrial base and highly skilled employment.

ev.amended: (b)Where the application of the requirements concerning Union origin and/or low-carbon requirements set forth in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III results in higher economic costs, contracting authorities shall ensure that such additional costs are duly and fully taken into account in determining the price schedules and cost bases underlying the performance of the works.
ev.justification: The amendment aim to ensure that the Union’s requirements regarding origin and low-carbon emissions are implemented in a proportionate and economically sustainable manner. Any additional costs arising from such requirements should be appropriately reflected in the pricing mechanisms used in public procurement, in order to safeguard fair competition and the economic balance of contracts. At the same time, their application should be aligned with actual market capacity and product availability, avoiding supply constraints, barriers to participation, and unintended distortions of competition.

ev.amended: (c)Contracting authorities shall ensure appropriate timing coordination between the application of the Union origin and low-carbon requirements set forth in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III and the availability of the relevant products on the market, taking into account market capacity and supply conditions, in order to ensure effective access for economic operators.
ev.justification: See above

ev.amended: (d)Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall not require small-volume manufacturers, as defined in Reg. EU 2019/631 Art. 10 paragraph 1, to meet the requirements set out in Annex III Part I, points (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f).
ev.justification: Small-volume manufacturers do not have the same capabilities of negotiations with big suppliers, both in terms of costs and delivery times. This amendment would preserve small-volume manufacturers with a production site in the EU, giving a specific flexibility as it is already the case in other regulations like type approval, CO2 emissions and EURO7.

ev.amended:
4a.Where a breach of the requirements set out in this Article has been established by a final decision of a competent authority, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall take appropriate measures in accordance with Union and national law, including exclusion from the public procurement procedure, termination of the contract, or other remedies provided for under applicable law and applicable collective agreements.
Where a beneficiary repeatedly breaches the obligations referred to in this Article, the contracting authorities and contracting entities shall recover all or part of the financial support granted and where appropriate, exclude the beneficiary from future public procurement procedures.

4a.For the purposes of paragraph 3, when assessing the availability of suitable tenders and the proportionality of applying the Union-origin and low-carbon requirements laid down in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall take due account of the availability of compliant products, Union manufacturing capacity and relevant supply conditions. The application of those requirements shall not prevent effective participation in procurement procedures where compliant products are not available in sufficient quantities or within the timeframe reasonably required for the performance of the contract.
ev.justification: An opt-in system only works if eligible components actually exist. The existing Article 11(3) safeguards should be applied in light of real manufacturing capacity and supply conditions, so EU-content rules create demand without making participation impossible where compliant products are temporarily unavailable.

ev.amended:
4a.Where the application of the requirements relating to Union origin and/or low-carbon requirements results in higher economic costs, contracting authorities shall ensure that such additional costs are duly and fully taken into account in the determination of price lists and cost bases underpinning the execution of works.
Contracting authorities shall ensure appropriate verification of the availability of the relevant products on the market, taking into account market capacity and supply conditions, in order to ensure effective access for economic operators.

4a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities may only decide not to apply the requirements set out in Annexes II and III, in whole or in part, on the grounds of excessive cost as specified in paragraph 3c of this article if the selected economic operator can demonstrate, through a self-declaration, or an equivalent document, that it has not benefitted from any of the categories of foreign subsidies laid out in article 5 of Regulation 2022/2560. The competent authority shall verify the information provided by the economic operator.

4a.Where a breach of the requirements set out in this Regulation has been established by a final decision of a competent authority, body or structure competent for those tasks, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall take appropriate measures in accordance with Union and national law, such as exclusion of the economic operator from the procurement procedure termination of the contract, exclusion from the procurement market for a certain period of time, or other remedies provided for under applicable law.

4a.Where circumvention is established after award, the contractor shall pay a charge of 10% to 30% of the contract value and the contract may be terminated, as provided for in the contract conditions.
On a second or any subsequent occasion within three years, the operator and any company controlled by the same beneficial owner shall be excluded from any procedure or support covered by this Regulation for a period of between one and three years.
ev.justification: A false declaration must have a consequence if the IAA wants to counter circumvention. The charge of 10% to 30% of contract value is taken from Regulation (EU) 2022/1031 [the International Procurement Instrument]. A second false declaration within three years leads to exclusion. Treating an inaccurate declaration as serious misrepresentation relies on the exclusion ground already in Article 57(4)(h) of Directive 2014/24/EU (the Public Procurement Directive), with its three-year limits and its self-cleaning safeguard under Article 57(6), so no new sanction is invented.

ev.amended: 4a.Where a breach of the requirements set out in this Article has been established by a final decision of a competent authority, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall take appropriate measures in accordance with Union and national law, including exclusion from the procurement procedure, termination of the contract, or other remedies provided for under applicable law.

4a.The requirements set out in this Article may also be applied to public procurement procedures not covered by Directives 2014/23/EU, 2014/24/EU or 2014/25/EU, including where their value is below the thresholds laid down in those Directives. Member States are free to decide whether to apply these requirements, provided that they comply with Union law.

4a.Where the application of Union origin requirements and/or low-carbon requirements set out in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III results in higher economic costs, contracting authorities shall ensure that such additional costs are duly and fully taken into account when establishing the price lists and cost bases underpinning the execution of the works.
ev.justification: Additional costs arising from Union origin and low-carbon requirements must be fully reflected in the price lists and cost bases used by contracting authorities. This is necessary to preserve fair competition and the economic balance of works contracts.

ev.amended: 4a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall not require manufacturers of new light commercial vehicles whose production sites are located on the territory of the Union and which fall below the applicable thresholds for small-volume manufacturers under Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/631 to meet the requirements set out in Annex II and III.

4a.Member States shall ensure that claims of Union origin and of low-carbon performance made for products covered by Annex II can be verified by the market surveillance authorities designated under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, and that contracting authorities and contracting entities may rely on the findings of those authorities.
ev.justification: Origin and low-carbon claims must be credible and enforceable. Market surveillance authorities should be able to verify them, so that contracting authorities can rely on their findings instead of carrying out checks themselves.

ev.amended: 4a.Where a contracting authority or contracting entity intends to rely on any of the conditions set out in points (a) to (d), the decision and its justification shall be determined before the launch of the procurement procedure and communicated in the procurement documents in a transparent and consistent manner.
ev.justification: Derogations should be decided and transparently justified before the procurement procedure is launched. This strengthens legal certainty, equal treatment and predictability for all economic operators.

ev.amended: 4a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall apply the requirements and conditions referred to in this Article in a proportionate manner, avoiding unnecessary administrative burden and undue restrictions on competition and access to public procurement.

4a.Contracting authorities and contracting entities or the relevant authority in the Member State shall continuously monitor the economic operators supplying products or services to ensure the compliance with the requirements set out in this Regulation.

4a.Regarding charging infrastructure, charging equipment should be considered as an integral component of electrified mobility for the purposes of the “Made in Europe” approach and public procurement rules.
ev.justification: Charging infrastructure should be considered an integral and indivisible part of the vehicle of the future and, consequently, of the European automotive value chain. Extending the “Made in Europe” approach and public procurement requirements to charging equipment would ensure consistency between policies supporting European vehicle manufacturing and those enabling its electrification. Beyond industrial considerations, European manufacturing can contribute to ensuring compliance with EU requirements on safety, cybersecurity, interoperability, data protection, reliability and appropriate service-level agreements (SLAs), which are increasingly critical as charging infrastructure becomes part of a connected and energy-integrated mobility system. The inclusion of charging equipment within the IAA “Made in Europe” framework would help to reduce strategic dependencies, strengthen European technological capabilities and supply-chain resilience, and preserve industrial investment, know-how and high-value employment in Europe.

ev.amended: 4a.The public procurement procedures set out in this Article shall be in line with the new Union public procurement rules.

4b.Final decisions adopted by a competent authority, body or structure competent for those tasks, establishing non-compliance of an economic operator with the requirements set out in this Regulation, shall be notified by the contracting authorities or contracting entities to the competent authority designated under Article 45 of Directive (EU) 2014/23, Article 83 of Directive (EU) 2014/24 and Article 99 of Directive (EU) 2014/25.
Upon notification, the competent authority shall inform the Commission of the final decision for alleged breach of the requirements under this Regulation.
The Commission shall, based on the information received, set up a database listing the non-compliant economic operators under this Regulation and link it to the Electronic Eligibility Service established pursuant to Article 133 of [Proposal for a Regulation on a Public Procurement Act].

ev.justification: Public procurement rules should place particular emphasis on facilitating SME participation through proportionate and simplified criteria. “Made in Europe” criteria should also take into account the impact on Europe’s industrial base and value chains, rather than focusing solely on the origin of the product.

ev.amended: 4b.Where a breach of the requirements set out in this Regulation has been established by a final decision of a competent authority, contracting authorities and contracting entities shall take appropriate measures in accordance with Union and national law, including exclusion from the procurement procedure, termination of the contract, or other remedies provided for under applicable law.

4b.Contracting authorities shall ensure appropriate temporal coordination between the application of Union origin and low-carbon requirements set out in Part I of Annex II and Part I of Annex III and the availability of the relevant products on the market, taking into account market capacity and supply conditions, in order to guarantee effective access for economic operators.
ev.justification: Application of Union origin and low-carbon requirements must be coordinated with actual market capacity and product availability, so that economic operators can obtain compliant products and participate effectively in procurement procedures.

ev.amended: 4b.This Article shall not apply to procurement procedures for goods, services or works directly necessary for the construction, operation or maintenance of electricity transmission systems, electricity distribution systems, gas transmission systems, gas distribution systems, hydrogen transmission networks or hydrogen distribution networks.
ev.justification: The amendment ensures that Union-origin and low-carbon requirements in public procurement remain effective while avoiding disproportionate costs, technical incompatibilities, supply constraints and material project delays. It strengthens legal certainty by requiring derogations to be determined and transparently communicated before the launch of the procurement procedure. Energy network infrastructure is excluded in order to safeguard security of supply, system reliability and the timely expansion of critical grids, while avoiding conflicting requirements with sector-specific energy legislation.

ev.amended: 4b.Contracting authorities and contracting entities shall comply with collective bargaining rules, in line with the principles set out in the laws of the Member States, in order to ensure fair competition and prevent social and wage dumping.

4b.The Commission shall issue guidelines to ensure consistent and transparent application of this Article, including on the determination of origin and the calculation of additional costs referred to in paragraph 3(c).

4c.The competent authority shall not require small-volume manufacturers of new electric light commercial vehicles, as defined in Reg. EU 2019/631 Art. 10 paragraph 1, with production site established and owned within the Union before the publication of the Proposal for the Industrial Accelerator Act, including R&D facilities, full engineering, highly skilled workforce, to meet the requirements set out in Annex II and III.

4c.This Article shall not apply to contracting authorities and contracting entities that are undertakings wholly or partly owned by public shareholders and that operate in the energy supply, network infrastructure or water sector, where the application of the requirements laid down in this Article would lead to market distortions in relation to comparable undertakings not subject to equivalent procurement requirements.
ev.justification: To preserve a level playing field, undertakings wholly or partly owned by public shareholders and operating in the energy, network infrastructure or water sector should not be subject to requirements that place them at a competitive disadvantage compared with comparable entities not subject to equivalent procurement obligations. This is particularly important where such requirements could delay or increase the cost of essential infrastructure investments.

ev.amended: 4c.The Commission shall make the list of partner countries for the purposes of this Regulation available through the publicly accessible online tool referred to in Article 71(1) of [Proposal for Public Procurement Act] and shall update the list whenever a third country is included or excluded as a partner country in accordance with this Regulation.

ev.original: Without prejudice to Articles 107 and 108 TFEU, Member States shall design public support schemes in a way that they contribute to the objective of strengthening the Union’s strategic industrial value chains through the Union origin requirements, low-carbon content requirements, or both, laid down in Part II of Annex II and Part II of Annex III, in accordance with Articles 9 and 10 and without prejudice to Article 13.
ev.amended:
Without prejudice to Articles 107 and 108 TFEU, Member States shall design public support schemes in a way that they contribute to the objective of strengthening the Union’s strategic industrial value chains through the Union origin requirements and low-carbon content requirements laid down in Part II of Annex II and Part II of Annex III, in accordance with Article 7, paragraphs 1 and 2 and Article 10 and without prejudice to Article 13 while ensuring that they comply with applicable social and labour law.
Companies benefiting public support schemes under this Regulation shall comply with social criteria aimed at creating and maintaining quality jobs. Such criteria shall include, where appropriate, obligations relating to site retention, employment guarantees, access to qualification and training measures, the promotion of workers’ participation, investment quota in productive capacity and long-term industrial activity or the application of collective agreements. Such conditions shall respect the varieties of social dialogue in Member States and not lead to undue discrimination against certain types of companies or Member States. Where relevant, Member States shall ensure that programmes and activities contribute to strengthening collective bargaining coverage and to improving working conditions in line with the objectives of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 on adequate minimum wages.
When designing such public support schemes benefiting companies, Member States shall include appropriate measures to prevent the relocation of manufacturing activities receiving support to outside the territory of the Union for a period of five years from the date on which the support is granted, or three years in the case of SMEs. Where a manufacturing activity receiving support relocates to outside the territory of the Union within that period, the competent authority shall recover the support granted.
Where a beneficiary materially fails to comply with commitments imposed pursuant to this Article, Member States shall take proportionate corrective measures, including, where appropriate, suspension, reduction or recovery of support. Serious, repeated or intentional non-compliance may result in temporary exclusion from public support under this Regulation.

ev.amended: Member States shall apply the requirements referred to in the first subparagraph to public support schemes accounting for 100% of the total national budget allocated to the public support schemes covered by Part II of Annex II and accounting for 100% of the total national budget allocated to the public support schemes covered by Part II of Annex III.
ev.justification: Public support should provide a clear and predictable demand signal for low-carbon and Union-origin products. The co-rapporteurs propose increasing from 45% to 90% the share of the national budget allocated to the public support schemes covered by Part II of Annex II to which these requirements apply. This amendment increases that share to 100%, so that the requirements apply to the entirety of the relevant support budget. This approach is justified, as public support schemes covered by Part II of Annex II already represent a targeted segment of the market. Applying the requirements to the entirety of the relevant support budget would maximise the leverage of public expenditure in creating lead markets for low-carbon and Union-origin products, without extending the requirements to the wider market. The targeted derogations already provided for in this Regulation ensure sufficient flexibility where compliance would result in disproportionate costs or significant delays, making an additional general exemption for part of the national budget unnecessary. It is also consistent with the treatment of public procurement, where the requirements apply in principle to all procurement procedures falling within the scope of this Regulation, subject to targeted derogations. By contrast, auctions are subject to a differentiated coverage requirement, reflecting their particular role in supporting the rapid deployment of net-zero technologies.

ev.amended: Member States shall also make sure, for a period of five years from the date of the final payment, that the intellectual property rights, know-how and manufacturing processes developed with recourse to public support granted under such a scheme are neither assigned nor licensed exclusively to an entity established in, or controlled from, a third country with a view to manufacturing outside the Union. ev.justification: Although public money is used to fund European innovation, once the technology becomes mature, the industrial manufacturing is increasingly being done outside the Union. ev.amended: 1a.By way of derogation from paragraph 1, Member States may decide not to apply the requirements referred to in that paragraph to public support schemes, or parts thereof, targeted at vulnerable households or at households in energy poverty or transport poverty within the meaning of Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2023/955, including measures financed by the Social Climate Fund, or at the construction or renovation of social and affordable housing.
ev.justification: Low-income families depend on support to replace old heating devices, renovate homes and buy clean vehicles. Origin and low-carbon requirements would raise prices and narrow choice exactly where affordability matters most. Social and affordable housing is financed from the same constrained public budgets and should benefit from the same derogation.

When designing and implementing public support schemes covered by this Article, the competent authorities shall take into account the need to avoid disproportionate differences in the ability of companies from different Member States to receive support, including as a result of differences in national fiscal capacity, and shall aim to ensure fair conditions of access to support for companies throughout the Union.
ev.justification: Articolul 12 cere deja ca autoritatea să evalueze contribuția produselor și tehnologiilor la obiectivul general printr-un proces deschis, nediscriminatoriu și transparent. Altfel, putem avea o schemă de sprijin care bifează criteriul „low-carbon”, dar contribuie prea puțin la dezvoltarea producției în România sau în alte regiuni mai puțin industrializate. Dacă o schemă de ajutor de stat este proiectată astfel încât cofinanțarea națională să fie foarte mare, statele cu bugete mai puternice pot sprijini mult mai ușor industria decât România. ev.justification: The text introduces a cost derogation mechanism that permits contracting authorities to bypass Made in EU requirements where compliance with the Act results in costs exceeding a 30% threshold. This raises significant concern that the regulation could be substantially weakened in practice. In the battery and electric vehicle sector, Chinese manufacturers often benefit from substantial state subsidies, vertically integrated supply chains, and large-scale production advantages. As a result, cost differences of 25–30% are not uncommon. Establishing the derogation threshold at this level risks turning the Made in EU preference from a mandatory requirement into a largely discretionary guideline. This framework may also encourage dumping behaviour, where goods are sold below normal value in order to trigger the cost-based exemption mechanism.

ev.amended: (b)would incur disproportionate costs. A difference in the cost of the underlying final product or technology alone shall not be sufficient to establish disproportionate costs. In particular, an initial cost differential arising during the establishment or scaling-up of Union manufacturing capacity shall not, in itself, constitute disproportionate costs. When assessing disproportionate costs, the competent authority shall take into account, where relevant, life-cycle costs, security of supply, resilience, strategic dependencies and the availability and prospective development of manufacturing capacity in the Union. ev.justification: The purpose of Union origin requirements in public support schemes is to strengthen strategic industrial value chains. An automatic cost-based presumption risks preventing newly established Union manufacturing capacity from reaching competitive scale and may perpetuate existing strategic dependencies

Raising the threshold to 50% would ensure that the derogation remains an exceptional safeguard rather than a systematic escape clause, while preserving the objective of anchoring industrial value creation in Europe.

(ba)where a company can demonstrate, on the basis of objective evidence, that the final product is primarily intended for non-EU markets; that its international competitors are not subject to equivalent requirements; that the mandatory use of European materials or components creates a cost differential that jeopardises the commercial viability of the offer; that no European alternatives are available in terms of quality, volume, delivery time or commercially reasonable price; or that strict application of the requirement could result in the loss of contracts, relocation of production, or substitution by non-EU competitors.
ev.justification: It is proposed that a specific international competitiveness clause be introduced to prevent European-origin or low-carbon requirements from placing companies operating in international markets at a competitive disadvantage. Such a clause should not undermine the objectives of decarbonisation or strategic autonomy, but should ensure that pursuing those objectives does not displace European companies from markets in which they remain competitive. The European-origin and European-content requirements envisaged under the IAA apply primarily to public procurement and other specific instruments and do not constitute a general obligation for products intended for international markets. Nevertheless, their application should remain proportionate and should not create unnecessary distortions affecting the competitiveness of European companies.

ev.justification: The amendment ensures that Union-origin and low-carbon requirements in public support schemes remain proportionate, predictable and investment-friendly. ev.justification: This issue is particularly relevant to the automotive sector, where technological transformation is having a significant impact on the European supplier network, many of whose businesses remain partly dependent on internal combustion engine technologies. It is therefore considered necessary to ensure a gradual and viable transition consistent with the preservation of industrial employment.

ev.amended: 3a.The competent authority shall not require manufacturers of new light commercial vehicles whose production sites are located on the territory of the Union and which fall below the applicable thresholds for small-volume manufacturers under Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/631 to meet the requirements set out in Annex II and III.

3a.would materially increase the cost to consumers by more than 20% for comparable models of zero and low-emission vehicles, significantly reduce the availability of affordable vehicle models or significantly hinder the achievement of national decarbonisation and zero-emission mobility objectives.
ev.justification: Member States should retain sufficient flexibility to design electric-vehicle support schemes around their specific market conditions, consumer purchasing power, transport needs, charging infrastructure and national decarbonisation pathways. A cost increase exceeding 20% for comparable models could place electric mobility beyond the reach of many households and businesses. This concern is particularly relevant for Malta, where households are highly dependent on private vehicles, the domestic market is small, vehicle choice may already be narrower than in larger Member States, etc. Restricting eligibility could further reduce competition, concentrate support among higher-priced vehicles and disadvantage lower- and middle-income consumers, SMEs, commercial fleets and public-service operators seeking to transition to cleaner mobility. The proposed safeguard would allow the competent authority to consider comparable vehicle prices, the availability of models across different market segments, delivery times, technical performance, charging compatibility, battery range, lifecycle costs and the expected contribution of the scheme to emissions reductions. It would also preserve technology neutrality by ensuring that support can remain open to the zero- and low-emission solutions best suited to national circumstances, rather than indirectly favouring a specific manufacturer, production location or technological configuration. The derogation would apply only where objective and transparent evidence demonstrates a material impact on affordability, consumer choice or achievement of national decarbonisation and zero-emission mobility objectives. A balanced approach would maintain incentives for European vehicle and battery production while recognising that the environmental benefits of support schemes depend primarily on the timely and broad adoption of cleaner vehicles.

ev.amended: 3a.The competent authority shall assess compliance with the requirements established pursuant to paragraph 1 of this Article on the basis of the self-declaration prepared in accordance with the standardized template set forth in the Commission implementing act referred to in Article 16(3).
ev.justification: Self-declaration is a useful tool for streamlining administrative burdens. A standardised template, particularly with regard to compliance with the new requirements on product origin, is essential to avoid imposing entirely disproportionate obligations on micro and small enterprises, including under public support schemes.

ev.amended: 3a.For vehicles, Member States shall verify compliance with this Article before granting support. They shall do so on the basis of the document referred to in Article 15, including the anti-circumvention self-assessment referred to in Article 7a.
ev.justification: Article 12 sets origin rules for vehicle subsidies, but nobody checks them. Car makers already issue a compliance document under Article 15, which now also contains the anti-circumvention check. Member States check that existing document before they pay, so there is no new paperwork.

ev.amended: 3a.This Article shall not apply to public support schemes where the financial support provided consists exclusively of promotional loans or guarantees.
ev.justification: Promotional loans and guarantees are important tools to mobilise private investment, including through national promotional banks. They should not be treated in the same way as direct public support and should therefore remain outside these requirements.

The amendment ensures that the granting of financial support is based on the actual economic cost of projects and equipment over their entire lifecycle, rather than solely on their purchase price. A comprehensive assessment encompassing the initial investment, operating and maintenance costs, durability, energy efficiency and operational availability will make it possible to identify the most cost-effective solutions, avoid disproportionate downstream costs and ensure the efficient use of Union resources. Furthermore, the establishment of harmonised methodologies by the Commission will ensure that these criteria are applied consistently, transparently and without discrimination across all Member States.

ev.amended: 3b.The competent authority shall not require small-volume manufacturers, as defined in Regulation EU 2019/631 Article 10 paragraph 1, with production site established and owned within the Union before the publication of the Proposal for the Industrial Accelerator Act, including R&D facilities, full engineering, highly skilled workforce, to meet the requirements set out in Annex II and III.
ev.justification: “Small-Volume Manufacturers” do not have the same capabilities of negotiations with big suppliers, both in terms of costs and delivery times. This amendment would preserve “Vans Small-Volume Manufacturers” with a production site in the EU, giving a specific flexibility as it is already the case in other regulations like type approval, CO2 emissions and EURO7

ev.amended: 3b.Where circumvention is established after the support has been granted, the support shall be reduced or recovered in accordance with the rules of the scheme.
ev.justification: If circumvention comes to light after a grant, the support is reduced or recovered under the scheme's rules.

ev.amended: This ‘made in the European Union’ criterion shall be considered equivalent to the ‘Union origin’ referred to in Article 7 of this Regulation and shall also take into account content equivalent to Union origin under Articles 8 and 9, where applicable.
ev.justification: Extending partner-origin recognition to vehicle-support schemes would ensure consistency with the broader “Made with Europe” approach established under Articles 8 and 9 and would prevent trusted partner content from being treated as automatically ineligible solely because it originates outside the Union. Modern vehicle and battery value chains are highly integrated and often depend on specialised components, critical raw materials, and other technologies sourced from reliable countries with which the Union maintains economic relations. Failing to recognise this could increase legal uncertainty for national authorities and economic operators, weaken the practical effectiveness of the partner-equivalence framework, restrict the range of eligible vehicles, reduce competition among manufacturers and importers, increase consumer prices and delay the uptake of zero- and low-emission mobility. These effects would be particularly significant for Malta, where the vehicle market is small, domestic manufacturing is absent, distribution and transport costs are comparatively high, and consumers already have access to a narrower selection of models than in larger Member States. Recognising qualifying partner content would allow support schemes to remain open to affordable and technologically suitable vehicles while maintaining incentives for Union production and investment. Eligibility should remain subject to the safeguards and criteria applicable under Articles 8 and 9. The recognition should therefore not amount to an unrestricted exemption for all third-country content, but should apply only where the partner relationship contributes to the Union’s economic security and strategic resilience.

ev.justification: The IAA should pair its requirements with incentives and additional funding that at least partially offset the increased costs of localising production, creating a genuine business case for manufacturing in the EU. At present, the most dependable incentive for cars and vans is the super-credit under the CO2 Regulation. Because it cannot be modified, cancelled, or withdrawn at Member State discretion, it offers manufacturers a degree of planning certainty the other mechanisms lack. Public support can be withdrawn by Member States or never granted in the first place. Furthermore, the proposal allows Member States to opt out of applying "Made in EU" provisions to public procurement and support schemes altogether, via the “escape clause” if it proves disproportionate costs. Effectively asking manufacturers to buy European while declining to hold public sector to the same standard. A manufacturer that has invested in local production and supply chain may see no reward for it, should a public authority simply choose to use that opt-out. Therefore, Extend the super-credit mechanism to other categories, including a super-credit of 1.3 to ALL zero-emission vehicles "Made in EU," not only small.

ev.justification: The proposed approach under the CO₂ emission performance standards does not create demand for low-carbon materials for all of the key materials needed to build a car. In particular, only steel is considered, while low-carbon aluminium is not included. This weakens policy alignment and sends a mixed signal to industry. Including low-carbon aluminium in the CO₂ credit system, alongside steel, would help ensure a more complete approach that supports the competitiveness of European value chains. This is particularly important when considering that electric vehicles tend to contain more aluminium than internal combustion engine cars (displacing steel), since aluminium is lighter than steel and lightweight EVs is crucial for improving the performance of the battery.

ev.original: This Chapter shall apply to foreign direct investments exceeding a value of EUR 100 million in the emerging strategic manufacturing sectors referred to in paragraph 2, where more than 40 % of the global manufacturing capacity is held by the third country of which the foreign investor is a national or undertaking.
ev.amended: This Chapter shall apply to foreign direct investments exceeding a value of EUR 100 million in the emerging strategic manufacturing sectors referred to in paragraph 2, where more than 40 % of the global manufacturing capacity is held by the third country of which the foreign investor is a national or undertaking, provided that the assessment also takes account of the contribution made by the investment to the Union’s security of supply, the diversification of supply chains, the development of production capacities, and added value created within the Union. The application of this chapter must not result in discouragement of foreign direct investments that make a significant contribution to the development of production capacities in the Union, the diversification of supply chains, technology transfer, job creation, and an increase in added value created within the Union. When assessing investments, competent authorities shall pay particular attention to the contribution made by the investment to the industrial development of less industrially developed regions.
ev.justification: Criteriul cantitativ de 40% poate identifica situații de concentrare a producției, dar nu reflectă, în sine, impactul concret al unei investiții asupra securității economice a Uniunii. Este necesară o evaluare care să țină seama și de contribuția efectivă a investiției la diversificarea surselor de aprovizionare, la dezvoltarea capacităților industriale și la crearea de valoare adăugată în Uniune. Amendamentul creează un argument juridic pentru ca investițiile productive în statele membre cu un nivel mai redus de dezvoltare industrială să fie evaluate și prin prisma contribuției lor la reindustrializare, crearea de locuri de muncă, transferul tehnologic și dezvoltarea lanțurilor valorice.

ev.amended: This Chapter shall apply to foreign direct investments exceeding a value of EUR 100 million in the emerging strategic manufacturing sectors referred to in paragraph 2.
ev.justification: A threshold of 40% of global manufacturing capacity would effectively mean that these provisions would only apply to Chinese companies. This approach does not protect against the takeover of strategic European assets by other countries. A more comprehensive approach would be to apply these FDI provisions horizontally to all foreign investors, regardless of their country of origin. This would ensure a level playing field and strengthen the EU’s capacity to safeguard its strategic industries in an increasingly turbulent global environment. The purpose should not be to exclude foreign investments, but rather to ensure that they are made in ways that create lasting value for both the EU economy and its citizens.

ev.amended: This Chapter shall apply to foreign direct investments made by a foreign investor or a foreign investor's subsidiary exceeding a value of EUR 50 million in the emerging strategic manufacturing sectors referred to in paragraph 2, where more than 20 % of the global manufacturing capacity is held by the third country of which the foreign investor is a national or undertaking.
ev.justification: A threshold of 40% of global manufacturing capacity is too narrow to ensure that major foreign direct investments genuinely strengthen the Union’s industrial capabilities rather than merely relocating production while reproducing existing strategic dependencies within the internal market. Strategic dependence and economic leverage may arise well before a third country reaches such an exceptionally high share of global production. This is particularly the case where significant concentration already exists in critical technologies, components, inputs or other bottlenecks within the relevant value chain. Setting the threshold at 40% risks activating the mechanism only once a strategic dependency is already deeply entrenched. Moreover, such a high threshold, particularly when combined with exemptions for countries covered by relevant international agreements, risks making an ostensibly horizontal economic-security instrument de facto applicable almost exclusively to investors originating from a single third country. This weakens the general and objective character of the mechanism, exposes it to accusations of discriminatory targeting and possible litigation or hostile coercive measures, while leaving comparable investment strategies from other significant manufacturing countries outside its scope. Lowering the threshold to 20% preserves a targeted approach while ensuring that the mechanism applies to countries already holding a substantial position in strategic value chains. It allows the Union to address dependencies before they become entrenched and ensure that foreign investment contributes to European industrial upgrading, technological capabilities and resilient supply chains, while maintaining openness to foreign investment.

The final decision to approve, revise or refuse a foreign direct investment shall remain with the competent Member State. In the case of decision not in line with the recommendation of the Investment Authority or the European Commission, the competent Member State shall issue a public statement justifying its decision.
ev.justification: FDI approvals should remain firmly under the competence and responsibility of the Member State in which the investment is made, as national authorities are best placed to assess its economic, security and strategic implications. Preserving the final decision at national level safeguards Member State sovereignty, avoids institutional duplication and ensures that assessments take proper account of national circumstances. A reasoned public statement where a Member State departs from a Commission or Investment Authority recommendation would nevertheless promote transparency, accountability and consistent application across the Union.

(1)This Chapter shall not apply to investors and investments covered by an economic partnership agreement, free trade agreement or customs union in force or provisionally applied by the Union, to the extent that relevant investment commitments exist under those agreements, including investments made by Union subsidiaries of such foreign investors.
ev.justification: This exemption would broaden Malta’s pool of reliable trading and investment partners by ensuring that investors covered by the Union’s economic partnership agreements, free trade agreements or customs unions are not subjected to duplicative or disproportionate screening requirements under the IAA. Where the Union has already negotiated relevant investment commitments and established a rules-based framework with a third country, those commitments should be recognised consistently in the application of this Regulation. Extending the exemption to investments made through Union subsidiaries would also reflect the commercial reality of integrated corporate structures and prevent formally EU-established entities from being disadvantaged solely because of the nationality of their ultimate investor. For a small, open and highly import-dependent economy such as Malta, maintaining access to diversified sources of capital, technology, expertise and supply-chain partnerships is essential for competitiveness and economic resilience. The amendment therefore supports legal certainty, avoids unnecessary administrative burdens and strengthens the Union’s credibility as a dependable trade and investment partner, while preserving the possibility of scrutiny where genuine security or strategic risks arise.

ev.amended: (2)For the purposes of determining the investment value under this Article, ordinary brownfield expansions, reinvestments and phased investments shall not be aggregated where they constitute separate investment decisions and do not materially alter the nature or control of the existing investment.
ev.justification: Ordinary brownfield expansions, reinvestments and phased investments should not automatically fall within the IAA FDI regime merely because the cumulative value of several distinct investment rounds exceeds the applicable threshold. Such investments are often part of the normal development of an established operation and may involve the gradual expansion of production capacity, modernisation of equipment, introduction of new technologies, energy-efficiency improvements or adaptation to changing market demand. Where each phase constitutes a separate commercial decision and does not materially alter the nature, ownership or control of the existing investment, aggregating all phases could create an artificial trigger for additional screening. This would generate legal uncertainty, increase administrative costs and potentially discourage foreign investors from expanding successful operations in the Union. The risk is particularly relevant for smaller economies such as Malta, where a limited number of sizeable industrial projects can have a disproportionately important role in employment, exports, skills development and technological upgrading. Providing clear protection for genuine brownfield expansions and evolving investments would therefore ensure that the mechanism remains focused on transactions presenting a real strategic or security concern, while supporting continued reinvestment, investor confidence and long-term industrial growth. The exemption should not apply where investments are deliberately divided to circumvent the threshold or where successive phases materially change the nature or control of the original investment.

ev.amended: 3a.The final decision to approve or decline a foreign direct investment falling within the scope of this Chapter shall remain with the competent Investment Authority of the Member State concerned. Without prejudice to the conditions laid down in this Chapter, the competent Investment Authority of the Member State concerned may impose additional conditions on the foreign direct investment, where it considers them necessary in accordance with national law, including for the protection of national security or strategic assets. Any assessment, coordination or opinion at Union level shall be without prejudice to those competences of the Investment Authority of the Member State concerned.
ev.justification: Member States should retain the final responsibility for foreign direct investments concerning their territory. The common Union framework should therefore establish minimum conditions without preventing national authorities from imposing additional requirements where necessary to protect national security or strategic assets.

ev.amended: 3a.The exclusion provided for in paragraph 3, point (c), shall not apply where, having regard to the scale or concentration of the shareholdings held, their cumulative or speculative nature, a situation of common ownership, concerted action by several investors or their combination with financing or contractual relationships, the investment is liable to exert significant influence over the undertaking concerned, the valuation of its assets, its financial stability or its capacity for long-term productive investment;

3a.This Chapter shall be without prejudice to applicable Union restrictive measures and to investment screening on grounds of security or public order under Union or national law. An approval under this Chapter shall not replace any authorisation required under such screening rules, prevent the imposition of security-related conditions, or prevent a Member State from prohibiting an investment on those grounds. The assessment shall take account of the ultimate ownership and control of the investor, including arrangements intended to circumvent the applicable rules.
ev.justification: Meeting industrial value-added conditions must not confer immunity from national-security screening. The amendment preserves national decisions and prevents investors from using intermediary structures to obscure ultimate control.

ev.amended: 3a.This Chapter shall be without prejudice to the responsibility of each Member State for its national security, in accordance with Article 4(2) TEU, or to the right of each Member State to protect its essential security interests in accordance with Article 346 TFEU. It shall apply in a manner consistent with national legislations and other Union legislation, including Regulation (EU) 2026/1386 on the screening of foreign investments in the Union [and repealing Regulation (EU) 2019/452].

3a.This Chapter shall not apply to a foreign direct investment in a Union target or Union asset that was completed, contractually committed, or authorised under Union or national law before the date of entry into force of this Regulation, nor to a same-site capacity expansion or technological upgrade of that investment that does not more than double its manufacturing capacity at that date.

3a.The Commission may, where appropriate and following an impact assessment and stakeholder consultation, submit a legislative proposal to amend the list of emerging strategic sectors covered by this Chapter.
ev.justification: Any extensions of the list of emerging strategic sectors covered by Chapter IV should be carefully assessed for possible negative effects, including reduced access to foreign capital and risk of disinvestments. To properly evaluate the impact of the provisions, the list should be amended via the legislative procedure, including impact assessment and stakeholder consultation, and not via a delegated act.

ev.amended: 3b.Where an investment, a series of investments, or a corporate structuring is carried out with no due cause or economic justification other than avoiding the application of this Chapter, including by splitting an investment to remain below the thresholds referred to in paragraph 1, this Chapter shall apply as if that circumvention had not taken place.

ev.original: 2.From [OP insert date: 12 month after entry into force of this Regulation], Investment Authorities shall only approve foreign direct investments made directly by foreign investors that fulfil either four or more of the following six conditions:
ev.amended: 2.From [OP insert date: 12 month after entry into force of this Regulation], Investment Authorities shall only approve foreign direct investments made directly by foreign investors that fulfil at least four of the conditions set out in this paragraph, on the basis of a proportionate assessment of the contribution made by the investment to security of supply, competitiveness, industrial capacity, employment, research and development, and value chain development within the Union.No condition shall be applied in a way that disproportionately leads to discouragement or prevention of an investment that makes a significant contribution to the development of the Union’s industrial capacities:
ev.justification: Regulamentul trebuie să urmărească atât securitatea economică, cât și atragerea investițiilor productive. Evaluarea trebuie să țină cont de contribuția efectivă a investiției și de caracteristicile sectorului și ale proiectului, nu exclusiv de îndeplinirea formală a unor criterii. Obiectivul de a crește ocuparea forței de muncă în Uniune este legitim, însă o cerință rigidă de 50% poate deveni o barieră pentru investițiile în sectoare tehnologice sau industriale în care există un deficit de competențe. Regula trebuie să stimuleze formarea și recrutarea lucrătorilor europeni, fără să transforme lipsa temporară a unor competențe specializate într-un motiv automat pentru respingerea investiției. Pentru o fabrică nouă, obligația de a atinge imediat un anumit procent din veniturile brute pentru cercetare și dezvoltare poate fi dificil de aplicat în primii ani, când investiția este concentrată în construcție, echipamente, punerea în funcțiune și formarea personalului. O perioadă de tranziție permite păstrarea obiectivului de dezvoltare tehnologică fără descurajarea investițiilor greenfield.

ev.amended: 2.From [OP insert date: 12 month after entry into force of this Regulation], Investment Authorities may, on a case-by-case and risk-based basis, take into account the following six conditions when assessing the contribution of the investment to the Union economy:
ev.justification: Ownership caps, joint-venture requirements, workforce quotas, technology-transfer commitments and local-content conditions may provide useful indicators when assessing the contribution of a foreign direct investment to the Union economy. However, they should guide a proportionate, case-by-case and risk-based assessment rather than operate as cumulative or mandatory approval tests. A rigid requirement to satisfy at least four of six conditions would treat investments with very different economic, technological and security characteristics in the same manner and could lead to the rejection of projects that deliver substantial benefits through employment, innovation, production capacity, supply-chain resilience or access to strategic technologies. It could also reduce the Union’s attractiveness as an investment destination by imposing prescriptive corporate structures and operational requirements that may be commercially unworkable or inappropriate for a particular sector. This concern is especially relevant for smaller Member States such as Malta, which rely on foreign investment to overcome limited domestic capital, skills and industrial scale. National authorities should therefore retain sufficient discretion to weigh the overall benefits and risks of each investment, taking account of the sector concerned, the investor’s profile, the availability of alternative suppliers, national labour-market conditions and the investment’s contribution to Union resilience. The proposed risk-based approach would preserve the ability to impose targeted and enforceable conditions where genuine economic-security concerns arise, while avoiding automatic requirements that could deter beneficial investment, delay projects or create disproportionate compliance costs.

ev.justification: While foreign direct investment falls within the scope of the Common Commercial Policy under Article 207 TFEU, the introduction of prescriptive value-added requirements, including ownership, workforce, joint venture and local content conditions, raises concerns regarding the limits of Union competence and the principles of conferral, subsidiarity and proportionality under Article 5 TEU. The proposed provisions resemble elements of an FDI screening framework and risk creating a de facto EU-level investment assessment and approval mechanism, potentially limiting Member State discretion in an area where national security remains a Member State competence. Evaluarea trebuie să țină cont de contribuția efectivă a investiției și de caracteristicile sectorului și ale proiectului, nu exclusiv de îndeplinirea formală a unor criterii. Obiectivul de a crește ocuparea forței de muncă în Uniune este legitim, însă o cerință rigidă de 50% poate deveni o barieră pentru investițiile în sectoare tehnologice sau industriale în care există un deficit de competențe. Regula trebuie să stimuleze formarea și recrutarea lucrătorilor europeni, fără să transforme lipsa temporară a unor competențe specializate într-un motiv automat pentru respingerea investiției. Pentru o fabrică nouă, obligația de a atinge imediat un anumit procent din veniturile brute pentru cercetare și dezvoltare poate fi dificil de aplicat în primii ani, când investiția este concentrată în construcție, echipamente, punerea în funcțiune și formarea personalului. O perioadă de tranziție permite păstrarea obiectivului de dezvoltare tehnologică fără descurajarea investițiilor greenfield.

ev.amended: (e)for each year from the implementation of the foreign direct investment and throughout its operation, at least 50% of the workforce employed in the context of the foreign direct investment, calculated on an average annual full-time-equivalent basis, shall be made up of Union workers. The 50% threshold referred to in the first sentence shall be calculated across the workforce as a whole and shall not apply separately to each category of the workforce, except in relation to research and development activities. Where the foreign direct investment includes research and development activities, the 50% threshold shall apply separately to each of the following categories of the research and development workforce, where present: scientific and technical functions, supervisory functions and managerial functions. Workers employed in research and development activities shall also be included in the overall workforce referred to in the first sentence. For the purposes of this point, a worker shall not be counted where the Investment Authority establishes, on the basis of objective and verifiable evidence and having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, that the recruitment or employment arrangement is non-genuine and has been put in place with the main purpose of artificially satisfying any 50% threshold laid down in this point. Union workers shall be employed across all categories of the workforce, including operational, technical, supervisory and managerial positions. Such employment shall be accompanied by adequate training and capacity-building measures. Where a Union target or Union asset already performing manufacturing activities before the investment is acquired, including after bankruptcy, maintaining the existing workforce or re-employment of the former workforce shall be prioritised, in accordance with national law and the application of collective agreements. In the event that the foreign investor, the Union target or the Union asset receives public funding, notwithstanding article 107 TFEU, it shall commit to maintain the share of the Union workers for a period of five years on pain of recovery by the relevant national authorities, the funding awarded;
ev.justification: The amendment defines the measurement and application of the 50% threshold, retaining its mandatory character under Article 18(3). It uses average annual full-time equivalents, includes research and development workers in the overall workforce and specifies separate thresholds for the listed research and development categories. A targeted anti-abuse rule concerns non-genuine arrangements, not the lawful acquisition of Union-worker status.

ev.justification: A fixed requirement that at least 50% of the workforce must consist of Union workers throughout the lifetime of an investment would be excessively rigid and may not reflect the labour-market conditions, demographic realities or availability of specialised skills in the Member State concerned. Foreign direct investments in strategic manufacturing frequently require highly specialised technical, engineering, managerial or operational expertise that may not be immediately available within the Union or in sufficient numbers at national level, particularly during the establishment and initial scaling-up of a project. This could therefore delay implementation, increase operating costs or discourage otherwise beneficial investments that would create employment, develop skills and strengthen the Union’s industrial capacity. The impact would be especially significant for small Member States such as Malta, where the domestic labour pool is limited and employers already rely on a combination of Union and third-country workers to address persistent skills shortages and sustain economic activity. The assessment should instead focus on the quality and durability of the investor’s overall contribution to employment in the Union. National authorities should retain discretion to define proportionate workforce commitments that reflect the scale, sector, maturity and location of the investment, as well as realistic recruitment conditions. Existing workers and former employees of acquired or restructured undertakings should remain appropriately protected. Replacing the fixed quota with a broader contribution-based test would therefore preserve the objective of generating tangible employment and skills benefits for the Union without undermining competitiveness, investment attractiveness or the timely delivery of strategic projects

ev.justification: Regulamentul trebuie să urmărească atât securitatea economică, cât și atragerea investițiilor productive. Evaluarea trebuie să țină cont de contribuția efectivă a investiției și de caracteristicile sectorului și ale proiectului, nu exclusiv de îndeplinirea formală a unor criterii. Obiectivul de a crește ocuparea forței de muncă în Uniune este legitim, însă o cerință rigidă de 50% poate deveni o barieră pentru investițiile în sectoare tehnologice sau industriale în care există un deficit de competențe. Regula trebuie să stimuleze formarea și recrutarea lucrătorilor europeni, fără să transforme lipsa temporară a unor competențe specializate într-un motiv automat pentru respingerea investiției. Pentru o fabrică nouă, obligația de a atinge imediat un anumit procent din veniturile brute pentru cercetare și dezvoltare poate fi dificil de aplicat în primii ani, când investiția este concentrată în construcție, echipamente, punerea în funcțiune și formarea personalului. Article21a
Review of foreign direct investments in other net-zero technologies
Where the foreign direct investment concerns technologies under points (a), (b), (d), (e), (h), (k) of Art. 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735, the following conditions shall apply:
(a) Investment Authorities may approve foreign direct investments made directly by foreign direct investors or foreign direct investors’ subsidiaries that fulfil the conditions set out in points (a), (e), (f) of Article 18 and in compliance with economic security objectives. Investment authorities may reject the proposed foreign direct investment if required by economic security objectives; in case of divergencies between the Investment Authorities and the Commission’s opinion even after additionally assessing the notification in greater detail, the Commission shall request the Investment Authorities to apply the conditions as per its opinion if this is necessary to avoid risks to the Union economic security.
(b) where the relevant Union targets or assets are located in more than one Member State, the Member States concerned shall coordinate the review of the relevant notifications and agree on the conditions to be applied with the other Member States, as well as with the Commission; the Commission shall decide which conditions shall be applied to the foreign direct investment where there is no agreement between the Member States concerned;
(c) all other provisions in Articles 18, 19, 20, 21 apply mutatis mutandis.

ev.original: (d)the Member State’s regions’ level of development, including least developed areas, regions in transition, and those undergoing industrial transformation.
ev.amended: (d)the Member State’s regions’ level of development and their potential contribution to strengthening the leadership of European industry in the sectors covered by this Regulation, with priority being given to regions undergoing industrial transformation.
ev.justification: It is essential to establish Industrial Manufacturing Acceleration Areas in territories undergoing industrial transformation to support a just transition. Priority should be given to regions with an established industrial base that require transformation to remain globally competitive, particularly in sectors such as chemicals and automotive manufacturing.To maximise the effectiveness and impact of Industrial Acceleration Areas, priority should also be given to territories with strong capabilities across multiple strategic sectors. The interconnection of these sectors through integrated value chains can enable faster and larger-scale progress in decarbonization and European industrial development. Consideration should also be given to territories with strong capacity to attract and retain talent linked to priority sectors, as well as significant potential for workforce reskilling and talent reconversion.

When carrying out its review, the Commission shall pay particular attention to the effectiveness of this Regulation and the persistence of the circumstances that have justified the adoption of this Regulation and to the necessity to introduce Union origin requirements for products from certain sectors critical to the Union’s economic security, notably the building of ships and of rail rolling stock.
ev.justification: the inclusion of a supply-adequacy check within the Article 29 review is essential as it addresses the fact that 'Made in Europe' requirements are calibrated against projected rather than existing manufacturing capacity. If EU supply of key components, most critically battery cells, fails to materialise at the scale and pace assumed, manufacturers will face binding obligations they cannot meet, driving up costs and undermining the competitiveness of EU-produced vehicles without any corresponding industrial benefit. A mandatory supply assessment at the three-year review, with the ability to adjust thresholds where shortfalls are identified, is therefore not a weakening of the Act's ambitions but a necessary safeguard to ensure those ambitions remain grounded in supply-chain reality.

ev.amended: By [OP: 12 months after entry into force of this Regulation], the Commission shall assess the introduction of an incentive mechanism into Regulation (EU) 2019/1242, in favour of zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles manufactured in the Union, and shall submit a legislative proposal, if applicable.

In the context of that review, the Commission shall systematically monitor the impacts on energy costs in order to ensure that the measures applicable in acceleration areas do not inadvertently increase industrial energy costs or undermine the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries.
ev.justification: The impact of IAA measures on energy costs should be monitored on an ongoing basis to ensure that implementation does not inadvertently raise industrial energy prices or erode the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries. Since energy companies are both regulated entities under the IAA and suppliers of energy to industrial users, energy price developments constitute an important element of the overall effectiveness assessment. Nuclear energy investments involve capital commitment horizons of 60-80 years and development cycles of 10-20 years. Subjecting nuclear-specific requirements to revision every 3 years or any short term time-frame creates regulatory instability incompatible with the investment certainty required for new nuclear builds, including SMR programmes. A 10-year review cycle is the minimum required for an adequate stable regulatory framework. In the automotive sector, given the complexity of supply chains and the pace of industrial transformation, the review should assess the actual availability, technical suitability and price competitiveness of Union-origin components. Where sufficient volumes of compliant components are not commercially available, or compliance would entail a disproportionate cost premium, appropriate flexibility should be provided to avoid undermining the competitiveness of Union manufacturers.

ev.justification: Article 26(1) sets generic auction criteria (business conduct, cyber security, delivery reliability, high-risk supplier exclusion) while Article 26(2a) separately mandates the technology-specific Union-origin criteria in Annex II (including BESS) whenever an auction covers a listed technology. Article 26(5)'s waiver for disproportionate costs or significant delays currently covers only paragraph 1 and not to 2a. So Member States have no clear basis to seek relief from BESS-specific criteria, unlike public procurement, where Article 25a(3) waives the equivalent Annex II obligation on the same grounds. This amendment adds paragraph 2a to the paragraph 5 waiver, aligning auctions with procurement.

(6a) The following article is inserted:
Article 28da
Partner origin
1. For the purposes of Articles 25a, 26, 28a and 28c, content of partner origin refers to content originating in:
(a) a third country that is Party to the Agreement on Government Procurement, provided that the procurement of the product in question falls within the scope of covered procurement under the Union's Appendix I to the Agreement on Government Procurement, taking into account the applicable Annexes;
(b) a third country with which the Union has concluded an agreement establishing a free trade area or a customs union, under the conditions laid down in that agreement, provided relevant obligations of the Union exist under the agreement for the product in question.
2. The origin of products and components shall be determined in accordance with Article 60 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council.
ev.justification: A consistent partner-origin framework is necessary across the Union-origin provisions applicable to strategic investment and Member State support. Extending this treatment to Article 28c reduces uncertainty for project developers and public authorities and avoids unnecessarily restricting established supply chains where relevant international obligations apply.

ev.justification: This amendment makes the recognition of third-country content as being of Union origin subject to clear conditions safeguarding reciprocity, fair competition, the Union’s economic security and climate commitments, while preventing circumvention. It extends this approach to Articles 25a, 26 and 28a, requiring national treatment for Union products or entities where comparable measures or schemes exist in the third country. Recognition must be withdrawn where the conditions are no longer met. For third countries meeting the additional criteria set out in points (i) to (iv), the amendment establishes a binding six-month deadline for the adoption of the relevant delegated acts, provided that all substantive conditions are fulfilled. This provides predictability for trading partners and businesses and supports timely implementation without weakening the safeguards governing eligibility.

ev.justification: The European supply chain of inverters, power plant control, battery management systems and assembly can be ready to meet the needs of new storage systems. Given the current concentration of global battery cell production outside the EU, introducing Union-origin requirements for cells from Phase 1 under Article 26 NZIA is crucial. Cells are the foundational component of a BESS, determining voltage profiles, thermal behavior, safe operating limits, degradation patterns, and system-level performance, including cybersecurity. Early requirements prevent formal compliance loopholes, such as partial offshoring or reliance on equivalent content, ensuring genuine EU-based manufacturing capacity. Introducing cells in the initial phase also provides a timely market signal, supporting rapid BESS deployment, investor readiness, and Europe’s industrial capacity, while strengthening strategic autonomy in net-zero technologies.

ev.amended: For battery energy storage systems, Member States shall not be required to apply the prequalification or award criteria laid down in Article 26, paragraph 2a where the battery energy storage system uses a battery chemistry for which the cumulative EU installed capacity does not exceed 5 Gigawatt at the time of publication of the auction procedure. ev.justification: Auctions are the primary route to market for large-scale BESS deployment, making the scope of Union origin criteria here particularly consequential. ev.amended:
(8a) In Annex II part III paragraph 1 point ca is added:
(ca)Electric charging technologies for transport: From [OP: Please insert the date = 2 years after entry into force of this Regulation], shore-side electricity supply equipment, and electric air transport supply equipment shall originate within the Union. In the case of electric vehicle supply equipment, Union localisation requirements shall be introduced progressively and differentiated by component, taking account of the actual availability of production capacity within the Union. Such availability shall be assessed through the mechanism established for that purpose in Article 7.
ev.justification: Charging infrastructure should be considered an integral and indivisible part of the vehicle of the future and, consequently, of the European automotive value chain. Extending the “Made in Europe” approach and public procurement requirements to charging equipment would ensure consistency between policies supporting European vehicle manufacturing and those enabling its electrification. Beyond industrial considerations, European manufacturing can contribute to ensuring compliance with EU requirements on safety, cybersecurity, interoperability, data protection, reliability and appropriate service-level agreements (SLAs), which are increasingly critical as charging infrastructure becomes part of a connected and energy-integrated mobility system.The inclusion of charging equipment within the IAA “Made in Europe” framework would help to reduce strategic dependencies, strengthen European technological capabilities and supply-chain resilience, and preserve industrial investment, know-how and high-value employment in Europe.
